channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Inside The Startup Building Uncensored AI (Abliteration AI) | EP 2345
gist: Devin Thomas of Abliteration (transcribed as 'obliteration') describes serving open-source models with refusals removed, plus customer-defined guardrail models, to cyber, red-team and Fortune 500 security buyers, as he estimates Chinese open models have closed to about three months behind the frontier and GPU supply limits his growth. The second half is an Ask Jason segment: AI won't kill the billable hour, AI-generated micro dramas are a cheap way to test IP and a Pixar-like AI studio is coming, and investors will still prefer co-founder teams over solo founders.

insights.claim: Devin Thomas's startup (rendered 'obliteration' in the transcript) serves open-source models with refusal guardrails removed to professionals in cyber, biology research, synthetic data and defense whom frontier labs underserve.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Shows that there is a real B2B niche serving legitimate users that frontier-lab safety policies turn away.
insights.quote: there's a whole bunch of uh professionals and companies out there that are essentially underserved or unserved by the frontier labs

insights.claim: Even large corporations enrolled in frontier labs' special cyber-access programs still complain about model refusals blocking routine security work, according to the founder.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Lab-run 'trusted access' programs leave enterprise demand unmet, which leaves room for third-party unrestricted providers.
insights.quote: It's still big corporations that have access to cyber programs are still having the issues with refusals

insights.claim: The company's main product idea is an 'inversion of control': an unrestricted knowledge model sits underneath a separate, small guardrail model where each customer writes its own policy, stricter or looser than the native one in different areas.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Splitting safety policy from the base model could become a common enterprise design and a product category of its own.
insights.quote: I always call it an inversion of control

insights.claim: The guardrail model is small enough to run in a few milliseconds, so routing each request through two models adds very little latency.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Small policy models make customer-defined moderation practical to run in production.

insights.claim: Abliteration works by using interpretability methods to find the parameters responsible for refusals and modifying them as little as possible, so the model loses little performance.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Removing safety tuning from open weights is cheap and repeatable, so model-level safety on open models is fragile.

insights.claim: The default policies the company keeps in place cover CSAM and self-harm.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Shows how far the 'uncensored' positioning actually goes, which matters for regulatory and reputational risk.

insights.claim: An early use case that worked is red-teaming the AI agents that banks and other critical-infrastructure firms are rolling out, for example trying to talk a bank's voice agent into wiring money out. Startup customers do this work under contract for those institutions.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: As enterprises deploy agents, they need adversarial testing tools, which creates a market for unrestricted models.

insights.claim: Testing your own systems against a newly published CVE is a typical request that big-lab models refuse and the unrestricted model answers.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Defensive security work is the clearest legitimate demand driver.

insights.claim: The founder estimates that Chinese open-source models such as GLM and DeepSeek have gone from roughly a year behind the absolute frontier to about three months behind.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: A shrinking lead weakens the moat behind frontier-lab valuations.
insights.quote: maybe before it was a year they were a year behind. I would say today they're maybe around three months behind

insights.claim: According to the founder, Anthropic recently published a blog post describing how capable GLM 5.3 is at cyber tasks, especially in its abliterated form, and that capability is part of the outrage in the industry.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Strong cyber capability in open models erodes the frontier labs' ability to restrict access to dangerous capabilities.

insights.claim: The founder argues that the term 'frontier model' wrongly implies a permanent ranking, and that models may commoditize to the point where end users can't tell them apart outside edge cases.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Commoditization puts pressure on margins for labs with high valuations and favors the application and infrastructure layers.
insights.quote: you have to worry about you know commoditization of models

insights.claim: Calacanis says frontier labs keep their newest models to themselves, so a defender such as Hugging Face could not use the same tools to defend against an attack driven by OpenAI's latest model.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Unequal access to capability is an argument for a market in independent offensive-security AI.

insights.claim: The founder thinks AI labs publicize their agents' hacking feats more than their white-hat patching work because 'if it bleeds, it leads': the hacks serve as capability marketing on social media.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Lab cyber disclosures double as marketing, so read them with that in mind.
insights.quote: if it bleeds, it leads type situation

insights.claim: Offensive-security benchmarks such as Exploit Gym reward models for how far they carry an exploit, which conflicts with any reward for stopping and alerting a human. The founder calls this an unsolved engineering problem for the whole industry.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Incentives built into how agents are trained create a structural risk of agents going too far, which is a source of liability.

insights.claim: The founder offers a 'boring' explanation for aggressive lab crawlers and agent overreach: big labs have so many researchers looking for impact that they keep raising the resources and challenges. Calacanis called it an insight he had never heard before.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Organizational sprawl at well-funded labs could lead to more legal and regulatory incidents.
insights.quote: They have how many x number of researchers, right? And I mean, they probably are looking for things to do

insights.claim: The startup's liability position is that it provides only 'information in, information out' with no agent layer, so the user is responsible, much as a hammer maker is not liable for an assault. A paid Stripe signup leaves a paper trail.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Unrestricted-model providers depend on a tool-maker liability theory that regulation could overturn.

insights.claim: Calacanis describes the President's AI announcement in Washington the previous week as telling companies to police themselves, with existing law and civil suits as the remedy for misuse.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A self-policing federal stance lowers the near-term regulatory risk for unrestricted-model startups.

insights.claim: Over the past month, Fortune 500 companies in almost every industry have contacted the startup, with CISOs wanting to test their own systems before outside AI attackers do. Before that, its market was mostly cyber and red-teaming startups.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Large-enterprise pull suggests unrestricted models are moving from a niche into mainstream security budgets.

insights.claim: The company grew so fast in the last two months that it ran out of compute and users complained it was slow; partners have since helped add capacity.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Shows how much demand there is and that access to compute limits AI startups' growth.

insights.claim: The founder says he used to think the GPU shortage was fake, but now finds that reliable, high-availability, high-performance GPU supply at scale is genuinely hard to get.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Firsthand evidence that GPU supply is still tight supports continued infrastructure demand.
insights.quote: I actually used to kind of think that the GPU shortage was fake

insights.claim: The company is in the Speedrun accelerator. Its founders came from big tech, it plans to stay B2B and leave consumer image and video use cases to others, and its stated goal is to be the trusted brand in unrestricted AI through audits and law-enforcement relationships.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: A focus on trust and compliance could set it apart in a 'wild west' category.

insights.claim: The founder cites an A16Z report finding that a large share of businesses have still not adopted AI, which he reads as large remaining upside outside the tech echo chamber.
insights.speaker: Devin Thomas
insights.so_what: Low enterprise adoption means a long runway of growth for AI vendors.

insights.claim: At Calacanis's own 20-person venture firm, the top 20% of people account for about 90% of AI usage, while the bottom half use almost none.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Uneven AI use inside firms points to opportunities in enablement and training tools.
insights.quote: why are these three people, you know, this top 20% using 90% and then the bottom half are doing nothing

insights.claim: Calacanis is skeptical that AI ends the billable hour. PCs, the internet and cloud computing didn't kill it; he expects experts to deliver more and better work per hour as humans move upstream, while commodity tasks such as convertible notes and trademark filings stop needing billable hours.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Counters the view that AI will wipe out professional-services revenue.
insights.quote: I don't buy that the billable hour goes away. I just think humans move upstream and do more important work

insights.claim: Calacanis argues that clients pay professionals to take ownership of a process and its liability, such as an auditor who will testify in a shareholder lawsuit, so a human stays in the loop even when AI can do the audit.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Accountability is a lasting moat for licensed professions.

insights.claim: Founder Matthew Kerbus of Practi argues that lawyers never dropped the billable hour because no technology made that easy, and hints that his company is building such a tool. He favors subscriptions over outcome-based pricing.
insights.speaker: Matthew Kerbus (caller, Practi founder)
insights.so_what: Pricing-model infrastructure for legal services is an emerging startup category.

insights.claim: A caller with Hollywood production experience says micro dramas, one to two hours of content split into 30 to 60 two-minute episodes behind a subscription, were shot live-action until about six months ago and are now made at scale with Seedance 2.5 and agent-driven ComfyUI pipelines.
insights.speaker: Bruno (caller)
insights.so_what: AI video has crossed into making commercial content at production scale.

insights.claim: Lon Harris says AI-generated romantic micro dramas get hundreds of millions of views, and TikTok runs a dedicated micro-drama app called Pine Drama that offers subscription and ad monetization.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: A new short-form video format with several revenue streams is growing quickly.

insights.claim: Harris says micro dramas are only practical because of AI: creators can generate sets, costumes and casts (for example, a royal ball in the 1500s) that would otherwise be too expensive.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: AI cuts production costs enough to make new formats economically viable.

insights.claim: Calacanis sees micro dramas mainly as a cheap way to test IP before taking it to other media, much as Marvel Comics tried short comic runs in the 1960s until hits like Spider-Man emerged.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Low-cost IP testing changes the economics of developing new franchises.

insights.claim: Calacanis predicts a 'Toy Story moment' for AI video, with a Pixar-like studio that combines AI with existing production tools rather than generating films from prompts alone. He thinks Jeffrey Katzenberg will be the one to figure it out.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Value in AI video may go to studios with strong storytelling, not to raw model providers.
insights.quote: We're going to have a Toy Story moment. Jeffrey Katzenberg is going to be the one who figures it out

insights.claim: Calacanis says Marvel let go of Andy Park, who led its visual development, along with his team, and that he has reached out to Park about starting a company. He sees laid-off top creative talent as a source of founders.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Studio layoffs may push top creative talent toward AI-native media startups.

insights.claim: Calacanis says AI won't change investors' preference for teams of two or three founders over solo founders. Co-founders can split the task-switching of the early stage, work without salaries, and remove the risk that one founder quits. Proven repeat founders such as Elon Musk or Travis Kalanick are the exception.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Shows how early-stage investors screen teams, even as AI makes a single founder more productive.

insights.claim: Calacanis's framework is that founders raise valuations by eliminating risks one at a time. A solo founder who reaches product-market fit on their own, for example a consumer product growing 5-10% week over week, removes enough risk to raise money.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: AI-enabled solo founders can get funded by proving traction before raising.
insights.quote: as I eliminate risk from this story then my valuation goes up
